newsitem.title: INDIA: Low rumbling in India rupee after RBI says overvalued.
newsitem.headline: Low rumbling in India rupee after RBI says overvalued.

text.p: The rupee weakened further on Tuesday against the forward dollar in the wake of comments by a senior central banker that the Indian currency was overvalued.

However, the spot rate was unmoved around 35.7100 rupees to the dollar, and it was too early to say that a long overdue correction in the exchange rate had started despite the rumblings in the forward market.
February-delivery dollars quoted at a premium of 1.05/1.08 rupees on Tuesday afternoon against last weekend's close of 0.88/0.90 rupees.
"It all started with the RBI's comments about the rupee's overvaluation at Goa," said one dealer.

Reserve Bank of India (RBI) deputy governor Y.V. Reddy told a meeting of foreign exchange dealers in the sourthern resort state on Friday that the rupee appeared overvalued based on an analysis of the real effective exchange rate.
Dealers said forward premiums started rising on Monday on corporate demand after Reddy's comments, and the trend gathered momentum on Tuesday afternoon as banks covered short positions.
"What happened was that there was some corporate demand based on Friday's statement," said a dealer at a European bank.
They said a stable rupee in the spot market will ensure that there is no panic covering by importers and the exchange rate will not change much unless corporate demand picks up further.
"If the recent rise in forward premiums had been due only to import demand, then we will be justified in thinking the correction has started," said the treasury head of a private sector bank.
"But a number of factors have contributed - some corporate demand, short-covering in the interbank market and tighter domestic liquidity," he said.
"When premiums first rose on Monday, stop-loss limits were triggered for some traders. This forced them to start covering and pushed premiums up further," the dealer said.
"Another factor which drove forward premiums up were high call money rates through last week," said another dealer. "This pushed up carrying costs."

Call money jumped to 7.5-8.0 percent last Tuesday from its previous close of 4.5-5.0 percent, after a central government bond auction drained 30 billion rupees. They remained at the same level through the week and hit 9.25 percent on Monday.
Dealers said they were uncertain whether market sentiment had been reversed.

The rupee has traded in a broad 35.70-35.90 per dollar range through the last year. Only Reserve Bank of India (RBI) dollar purchases have kept it from strengthening on the back of strong foreign capital inflows and poor demand for the U.S. currency.
"Some corporates have started covering but I think the real rush (for booking forward cover) will come only if the rupee weakens in a big way," said a dealer.
Dealers said the RBI has concentrated on the forward market in recent times as intervention in spot increases money supply and stokes inflation.

The RBI's intervention in the spot-market, by purchasing dollars to check the rupee's rise, pumps rupees into the banking system. It has bought $4.6 billion dollars in the first four months of the current fiscal, beginning April 1.
The latest RBI data shows year-on-year M3 growth at 16.7 percent for the fortnight ended July 18 against the target of 15.0-15.5 set for 1997/98 (April-March).
